This study introduces a novel approach for local image feature matching that leverages the Transformer architecture to enhance the effectiveness of existing deep learning methods. By applying self-attention to local image features, the method effectively aggregates context from both spatial and channel dimensions, allowing it to focus on matching corresponding points even in low-texture regions. We evaluated our model on the MPI Sintel dataset for dense matching and the Oxford, Pascal, and COCO datasets for detection tasks. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly boosts the performance of state-of-the-art matching algorithms. Furthermore, we released the project's code and pre-trained models at https://github.com/zhengruixu/TransformerMatching.

We investigate the causes of the significant discrepancy between the $B_\perp$ distributions derived from the two polarizations of the MUSE instrument on the VLT. Our analysis reveals that the bias affecting the measurement of the component of the magnetic field perpendicular to the line-of-sight stems from a combination of the spatial distribution of the line-of-sight component ($B_\parallel$) and the varying orientation of the polarizer within the instrument. Consequently, the observed polarization degree is inherently biased by the relative alignment of the applied polarizer and the actual magnetic field direction. This study provides a detailed examination of the specific sources of this bias and outlines a method for correcting the data.

This paper examines a network comprising multiple consumers and generators, analyzing how each rational participant maximizes their own utility. The research focuses specifically on the impact of time-of-use pricing on consumer behavior, designed to incentivize consumers to reduce energy use during peak periods by shifting consumption to off-peak times. This strategy aims to mitigate demand surges during high-load intervals and alleviate strain on the power grid. The analysis establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for equilibrium, demonstrating that both individual consumer strategies and aggregate system loads can be effectively modeled as a convex optimization problem. Furthermore, the study derives specific conditions ensuring that the Nash equilibrium results in an optimal outcome for the entire system.

This study examines the thermodynamic characteristics of charged black strings situated within Einstein-Maxwell theory, specifically utilizing the framework of Brans-Dicke gravity. By employing a canonical ensemble approach, we calculate the Hawking temperature and analyze the gravitational analogues of electric field intensity, free energy, and entropy. Furthermore, we investigate mass and charge fluctuations across various fixed horizons, evaluating their impact on the system's thermodynamic behavior.

This work examines ergodic theorems within the framework of spectral theory. It demonstrates that the power-law decay exponents specified in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem correspond precisely to the pointwise scaling exponents of an associated spectral measure. Furthermore, the study establishes ergodic conditions capable of yielding quantitative rates for the strong convergence of ergodic averages, which are then illustrated through various examples.

The study of Galactic chemical evolution and star formation relies heavily on metal-poor stars, which are often difficult to identify. This research reports the discovery of a new metal-poor star, designated J0828+3632, through the J-SNAP spectroscopic survey. The star exhibits a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -2.75 ± 0.05 dex and an abundance ratio of [α/Fe] = 0.40 ± 0.10 dex. Located at a heliocentric distance of 174 ± 1 parsecs, it is the closest metal-poor star identified to date by this survey. The analysis reveals that the star is α-enhanced, and its abundance patterns align with those of the Galactic thick disk. Furthermore, the study indicates that the star's kinematics are consistent with membership in the Galactic thick disk.

Global fire season lengths were assessed using MODIS hot spot data from 2000 to 2019, revealing that most regions have seasons extending no further than 12 months. However, notable exceptions exist in South America and Siberia, where seasons can persist for up to 18 months. A significant decline in fire activity occurred in South America between 2000 and 2019, a trend driven by shorter fire seasons rather than a reduction in monthly intensity. Conversely, Siberia experienced an increase in fire activity during the same period, resulting from a rise in the number of months with hot spots rather than heightened intensity.

Morphological complexity is a fundamental metric for quantifying the structural intricacy of a language, yet its precise definition and calculation methods remain subjects of significant debate. This study investigates complexity complexity by analyzing morphological complexity across 1,000 randomly sampled regular expressions, each representing a unique language from the regular family. The analysis focuses on four distinct measures: the lengths of the shortest generators, the lengths of the most concise representations in four different regular expression dialects, the dimensions of the underlying automata, and the magnitudes of their state-transition matrices. The results indicate that the first principal component accounts for over 90% of the variance in these complexity measures. Furthermore, the relationships between different measures are highly correlated, and they all exhibit strong positive correlations with corpus length and training duration. These findings suggest that various morphological complexity metrics capture essentially the same underlying dimension of linguistic structure.

We investigate the impact of self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) on the substructure population within the Milky Way. Our findings indicate that while SIDM does not significantly alter the number of substructures compared to standard cold dark matter (CDM), it does modify their internal density profiles, specifically flattening their central cusps. Consequently, the observed phase shifts in substructure orbits relative to CDM predictions are reduced. This effect could help resolve discrepancies regarding the lack of observed orbital lags in globular clusters that are otherwise expected in a CDM framework.

This study introduces a novel method for approximating subspaces within model order reduction frameworks for parametric partial differential equations. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on solutions from a limited set of sampled parameter values, our technique integrates data from the full set of parametric values alongside solution samples. By utilizing a solution operator to generate a specific flow of these samples, the resulting subspace is derived from the invariant characteristics of this flow. We demonstrate that this approach offers theoretical advantages over standard methods and validate its practical efficacy through numerical experiments on the parametric Stokes equations and a parametric advection-diffusion equation.

This study introduces the m-ar-RFA-KFastica method, a novel technique for extracting features from noisy environments. The method employs a binary matrix to generate a sparse representation of input data, enabling the handling of incomplete information through the use of a learned mask. A new objective function is derived to maximize non-Gaussianity in these features, incorporating both mean and median statistics to enhance robustness against outliers. The optimization process utilizes the ar-proximal gradient method, which guarantees convergence to a stable solution. The learned mask is then applied to achieve effective feature extraction. Experimental evaluations confirm that the proposed RFA-RFA-KFastica method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness.

Social media streams offer a timely and cost-effective method for identifying events, ranging from natural disasters and political uprisings to product launches and celebrity scandals. However, the sheer volume of generated content makes it difficult to pinpoint the precise origin of these topics. This paper introduces a novel framework for locating the geographical source of significant social media events by analyzing the structural characteristics of the information diffusion process. We evaluate the proposed method against two existing baselines using event data extracted from Twitter. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance in pinpointing the geographical origin of these events.

This paper demonstrates that very weak solutions to certain nonlinear variational elliptic PDEs—specifically those driven by $\mathcal{A}(x)$—are automatically Lipschitz-continuous provided the coefficient matrix $\mathcal{A}(x)$ is Lipschitz-continuous itself. This result extends the earlier work of Chiappal1oni, Giusti, and Miranda (1952), which focused on the constant coefficient case $\nabla \otimes f(x)$, and further generalizes recent findings by Chen, Li, and Wang (2020) concerning symmetric matrices. A distinctive feature of our contribution is the removal of any constraints on the growth or integrability conditions of $\mathcal{A}(x)$.

The recent discovery of a cobalt-rich ($\text{Co}_{0.92}\text{Ni}_{0.08}\text{WS}_4$) antiperovskite magnet prompts a re-evaluation of antiperovskite magnetism, specifically focusing on cobalt-rich variants. Our analysis reveals that the stability of cobalt-rich compounds is driven by a high entropy of formation, which is intrinsically linked to their high magnetic moments. This phenomenon is further supported by a strong ferromagnetic moment that effectively suppresses the antiferromagnetic state. We identify $\text{CoNi}_3\text{WS}_4$ as a highly stable cobalt-rich candidate, possessing a Curie temperature ($T_c$) of 1010 K and a saturation magnetization of 2.61 $\mu\text{B}/\text{f.u.}$ at 5 K. Furthermore, $\text{CoNi}_3\text{WS}_4$ exhibits a giant magnetocaloric effect, with a maximum value of $|\Delta \Sigma_{max}| = 11.8$ J/kg·K at 300 K under a magnetic field change of 2 T. These findings underscore the potential of cobalt-rich antiperovskites for applications in both spintronics and magnetic refrigeration.

Real-time bidding (RTB) has become a dominant model for delivering online digital advertisements. Within this framework, ad slots are sold to the highest bidder on a millisecond basis, necessitating that buyers submit bids for every impression dynamically. This paper examines how the buyers' risk preferences influence bidding strategies, specifically analyzing how the risk of underpayment to sellers and the risk of overpayment affect bidding decisions. We introduce a Risk-Aware Q-Learning (RAQ-Learning) approach grounded in Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) to optimize bidding strategies. Our findings indicate that while risk-neutral bidding yields suboptimal returns under certain conditions, incorporating CPT-based risk preferences can significantly enhance revenue. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of various CPT parameters on performance, demonstrating that optimal outcomes depend heavily on specific parameter settings.

Quantum wigner negativity serves as a marker of non-classicality within individual systems, while quantum steering acts as a precursor to non-locality in shared systems. This study examines the relationship between these two phenomena, revealing that if one subsystem exhibits Wigner negativity conditioned on another subsystem's Wigner positivity, then the two subsystems must exhibit quantum steering. Furthermore, we derive a specific criterion for detecting this type of steering solely through Wigner function representations. Our analysis also demonstrates that Wigner negativity can arise in subsystems even when the broader state is unsteerable. These theoretical findings are validated through experiments involving photonic displacement operations and homodyne detection, utilizing specific classes of multimode Gaussian states.

We assess the randomness quality within a commercial, random-number seed (RNS) module integrated into a 100-meter, 1-Gbps commercial-grade four-mode discrete modulation quantum key distribution (DM-DQKD) system. Our analysis employs entropy evaluation to determine security bounds and entropy tests to verify the randomness of an RNS. Additionally, we examine entropy variation under different light intensity levels and the correlation between entropy and error rates. Results indicate that non-uniformity in the RNS significantly impacts the secure key bound, whereas the RNS exhibits entropy values consistent with the expected theoretical limits across light intensities, showing no significant correlation with error rates.

This paper explores the geometry of timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curves situated in four-dimensional Minkowski space. Initially, we establish the definition of these specific higher-dimensional curves. Subsequently, we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing them and categorize them into distinct types. Finally, we provide concrete examples to illustrate each identified example.

This work examines Feller's diffusion, a population model characterized by immigration and isolation effects. The isolation mechanism is defined by an individual's propensity to relocate to a random location within the unit interval. We demonstrate that the model's density function can be represented as a series expansion involving shifted Laguerre polynomials, where the coefficients are determined by a Poisson point process on the positive real line $\mathbb{R}_+$. This series converges in mean square for all times $t > 0$ and spatial positions $x$ within the open interval $(0,1)$. Additionally, we establish a large deviation principle for a specific random series arising in Feller's model.

This study presents a comprehensive and unified framework for investigating single and multiphoton scattering phenomena in waveguide quantum electrodynamics (waveguide QED). The proposed framework relies on the utilization of effective vertex functions, which act as compact three-point building blocks representing the interaction between a quantum system and the electromagnetic field. These functions are determined by a dedicated numerical procedure and enable the application of diagrammatic perturbation theory using streamlined analytical expressions. The approach is particularly effective for analyzing near-resonant two-photon interactions, a scenario often neglected in previous research. The resulting theory is highly versatile, accommodating various quantum optical architectures, including linear and ring waveguide configurations, as well as systems featuring multiple emitters. The validity of the proposed framework is verified through a detailed analysis of two-photon near-resonant scattering within a waveguide qubit model. The findings reveal that two-photon scattering processes are intrinsically linked to the system's eigenstates and their corresponding eigenenergies. The framework further facilitates the analysis of multiphoton interactions in ring waveguide setups involving multiple emitters, offering a clear description of how scattering events modify the system's effective parameters.

We introduce a novel methodology to investigate spin-dependent scattering of boosted dark matter (BDM) off nucleons, wherein interactions are mediated by a light bosonic mediator. Unlike conventional approaches, our framework explicitly accounts for the finite lifetime of the process by incorporating the time component of the proton structure form factor. This becomes critical in scenarios where the BDM-mediator-proton interaction is resonant. Our analysis reveals that the temporal contribution substantially modifies scattering cross-sections in the non-relativistic regime, leading to significant alterations in the resonance profile. These findings offer new avenues for interpreting results from the LUXE experiment and similar initiatives investigating BDM.

In this paper, we introduce a recursive formula for computing the numerical coefficients of the generating function associated with the odd Bernoulli numbers, and we demonstrate it using a proof based on Taylor series expansion.

Conventional non-coherent differential detection offers an attractive balance by offering a simple receiver architecture while avoiding the need for a phase-lock loop. However, this approach results in significant performance degradation in continuous phase modulation (CPM) schemes. This paper introduces a new differential detector that achieves a substantial performance enhancement for CPM. The proposed method functions as a differential detector with phase mapping; it rearranges the input data stream to generate data symbols that correspond one-to-one with the received signal, thereby enabling more effective reception. The paper analyzes the bit error rate (BER) performance of this detector across both additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and Rayleigh fading channels. The study demonstrates that for several common CPM configurations, the proposed detector achieves near-optimal performance with negligible implementation complexity.

Reinforcement learning from neural network output interpretations (RTRL) represents a reward learning approach that trains models by integrating human feedback, yet it suffers from limitations such as the need for extensive data collection and high annotation costs. To overcome these hurdles, we present Reward Learning with Natural Language Feedback via Graphical Analysis (RL-GNN), a novel framework designed to elicit and integrate subjective user preferences more effectively. Our method models the reward function as a graph structure where nodes represent features and edges represent feature interactions, enabling the extraction of granular policy updates from coarse human instructions. By leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) for representation learning, we capture feature relationships and facilitate the seamless integration of individual bit-level preference signals. Empirical evaluations on a variety of benchmark tasks demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses existing methods in both sample efficiency and performance.

We introduce a new parametrization of nucleon structure functions, leveraging extensive experimental datasets from deep inelastic scattering, neutrino-nucleus interactions, and parity-violating electron scattering. Our parametrization aligns with the latest global fits for parton distribution functions and accounts for the most recent lattice QCD findings regarding nucleon spin. Additionally, we present the most precise estimates to date of the axial radius of the neutron.

We introduce a novel adjustable frustrated Toric code that permits tunable zero-energy excitations within its fluxes. This model exhibits a first-order phase transition between two distinct topological phases, each possessing an extensive number of degenerate ground states. By employing a mapping to the 3D classical torus partition function, our findings establish a one-to-one correspondence between this quantum code's transition and that observed in chromoelectric theory. Furthermore, utilizing a quantum real-space renormalization group approach, we demonstrate that the transition temperature is proportional to the energy gap separating the two topological sectors. Finally, our analysis reveals that the model's degeneracy can be reduced to a polynomial order through a specific construction.

We demonstrate that, provided the maximum off-diagonal decay rate is slower than a square-root sequence, the Gaussian Unitary and Orthogonal Ensembles, respectively, are universal limits for the eigenvalues of non-zero imaginary parts of large random Hermitian matrices. This result holds regardless of the specific distribution, as long as the bandwidth grows faster than the square-root sequence.

We introduce a new approach to training dialogue models using Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) as an abstract representation of the semantic space. By leveraging the inherent symbolic nature of AMR, our method facilitates the integration of a symbolic loss function, enabling the training of neural models with formal guarantees regarding their logical correctness. We demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MultiWOE 2.0 benchmark, surpassing purely symbolic baselines by delivering both higher accuracy and greater interpretability.

Understanding how algorithms reach their conclusions is a critical component of AI safety, yet the field currently lacks a unified approach to quantify interpretability. This study introduces a conceptual framework for measuring algorithmic interpretability that is intended for comprehensive evaluation of existing metrics and the development of future ones. The proposed model defines human understanding of automated decisions as a graph traversal, where nodes represent potential human beliefs and directed edges signify the relative importance of those beliefs in guiding human action. The authors argue that an effective measurement tool must be precise, unbiased, and capable of distinguishing between distinct types of interpretability. Additionally, the study introduces a qualitative taxonomy of interpretability and a set of criteria for assessing qualitative metrics. The authors demonstrate how their measurement framework can be applied to existing quantitative interpretability tools, identifying specific limitations and proposing directions for improvement. Finally, the authors apply this new model to a real-world scenario: evaluating the interpretability of a loan-approval algorithm from the perspective of a human applicant.

Although an extensive body of work exists on deep learning-based methods for detecting anomalies in time series data, these techniques typically depend on expensive and labor-intensive labels. This paper introduces Time Series Anomaly Detection with Weak Labels (TSAD-WL), a novel approach that leverages the vast quantity of time series data available with limited labeling constraints. TSAD-WL utilizes three types of weak labels: time series segments marked as anomalous, segments identified as normal, and full normal time series. The method employs a specialized loss function to train a neural network that learns to distinguish between anomaly segments and normal segments, while simultaneously constraining the network to produce higher output values for anomaly segments and lower values for normal segments. This process effectively trains a classifier to isolate anomaly segments from normal ones. Subsequently, the system applies the trained classifier to all normal segments of a target time series to detect anomalies, while also incorporating the original anomaly labels to refine final results. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that TSAD-WL significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, even when provided with just 10% of the data labeled as anomaly segments.

The choice of domain and the associated model are pivotal in extreme value analysis. Extreme value theory (EVT) offers two primary approaches: the block maximum method, which analyzes statistics from disjoint blocks of data, and the peaks-over-threshold (POT) method, which examines data exceeding a specified threshold. While the POT method is more flexible, its reliance on selecting an optimal threshold introduces challenges. This paper introduces a novel class of distributions termed "threshold-invariant," designed to eliminate the need for threshold selection by leveraging the natural independence found in threshold-excess data within threshold-invariant models. We evaluate these models against existing distributions, including the generalized Pareto distribution (GPD), demonstrating that GPD performs suboptimally compared to our new approach.

The study derives exact formulas for the average cross-sectional area of a 2D shape viewed from random directions in 3D space and the average projected surface area of a 3D shape viewed from random lines. It further establishes the conditions under which the average cross-section of a 2D shape reaches its maximum and determines the relationship between average projected area and average diameter for a 3D object. Finally, the paper presents specific cases including average projected areas for ellipses and triangles, as well as average diameters for disks and squares.

Commonsense knowledge graphs (CSKG) are designed to model vast networks of commonsense knowledge, serving as a vital resource for advancing natural language understanding. However, current methods for generating CSKGs often rely on labor-intensive human annotations or are restricted to narrow knowledge domains. This paper introduces a novel approach that automatically infers relations within a CSKG by leveraging knowledge from large language models (LLMs). Our method employs an innovative architecture featuring a semantic memory bank and a specialized memory-aware decoder. This design enables the retrieval of relevant knowledge from an LLM and facilitates the direct generation of relation triples. Experimental results indicate that our approach significantly surpasses existing baselines in terms of precision, recall, and F1 scores. Furthermore, analyses of generated samples demonstrate that our method produces high-quality relation triples with minimal errors.

The Hi-GAL initiative, led by the Herschel satellite, focuses on a comprehensive census of the Milky Way's star-forming regions by mapping them across three infrared bands: 250, 350, and 500 micrometers. This survey targets dust heated by young stellar objects and protostars, which serves as a key indicator of recent star formation activity. This study introduces the methodology for creating a catalog of point sources within the Hi-GAL survey's first data release, covering the Cygnus region at wavelengths of 250 and 350 micrometers. We employ a cataloging algorithm that utilizes a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach to estimate the probability density functions for point source fluxes and positions. To ensure accuracy, we assess the algorithm's performance through simulations and a dedicated analysis of the nearby Taurus-Auriga star-forming complex. Additionally, we apply the method to derive catalog entries for the Cygnus area, utilizing both the complete survey dataset and a high-resolution sub-region centered on the Cygnus X complex.

Chromosphere maps of the globular cluster NGC 1851, created using the Hubble Space Telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) in the near-UV range, reveal two distinct populations of red giants: an inner group with iron-poor compositions and an outer one with iron-rich compositions. Red giants located within the cluster's core exhibit lower iron abundances and are positioned more negatively on the chromosome map, whereas outer members show higher iron abundances and less negative map positions. This observed trend aligns with previous findings from the Magellan Observatory, which utilized near-infrared spectroscopy to study the same cluster. The dual-population structure of NGC 1851 mirrors those found in other globular clusters, such as 47 Tucanae, suggesting that the chromosome map technique offers a promising method for identifying multiple stellar populations in similar systems.

This study examines an overdangled ideal single-file system featuring two absorbing boundaries, with initial particle positions drawn from a Poisson distribution. By applying the theory of partial differential equations, we derive the exact survival probability and the conditional density function for particle displacement given survival. Our findings demonstrate that the survival probability adheres to a universal power law, the exponent of which relies solely on the total number of particles. Furthermore, we calculate the mean and mean squared displacement for surviving particles, revealing that the latter grows linearly with time, thereby characterizing the surviving distribution as a spreading Gaussian profile.

Although classical Bayes' rule is widely recognized as the standard framework for quantum state updates, its application to measurement outcomes in the quantum realm remains a subject of debate. This study demonstrates that classical Bayes' rule cannot adequately capture the causal influence of measurement actions on quantum systems. Furthermore, we show that a modified version of quantum Bayes' rule can address these limitations, effectively incorporating the necessary update for measurement-induced changes.

This study derives leading-order finite-size corrections to the equation of state, boundary free energy, and entanglement entropy, utilizing the holographic framework for systems governed by a $c$-extremal principle. Leverishing these results, we examine the behavior of the entropy of an entanglement cut situated near the boundary and investigate the physics of the boundary itself.

Let $\eta$ denote the algebraic transfer map from the cohomology of the Steenrod algebra to the cohomology of the Lie algebra associated with the Steenrod algebra. This map constructs an invariant under a specific equivalence relation. This paper investigates the linear independence of certain Ext-groups derived via the algebraic transfer. By analyzing these transfers, the linear independence of some of these Ext-groups is established.

The Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Instrument (FUSE) is designed to observe the far ultraviolet (FUV) spectrum, spanning wavelengths from 90 to 200 nanometers. This capability stems from its use of a grating spectrometer paired with a hydrogen absorption cell, a setup that inherently blocks radiation below approximately 110 nanometers. This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling the instrument's spectral response, which explicitly incorporates the absorption characteristics of the hydrogen cell. By leveraging the FUSE Light Curve Monitor (LCM) data, the study constructs a comprehensive model of FUSE's spectral response. This model serves as a robust tool for accurately deconvolving observed spectra, thereby enabling the recovery of source emission profiles with a significantly extended short-wavelength cutoff. The proposed methodology is validated through the analysis of the spectrum of the star BD+17 2596. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the incoherent scattered light observed in FUV spectra can be effectively explained as light reflected off the grating and subsequently filtered by the hydrogen cell.

This paper introduces a new class of distributed optimal control problems known as Graph Symmetric Systems (GSSs), which are governed by specific types of graph symmetries. We demonstrate that the optimal cost for these GSSs can be effectively computed using standard model-based methods. Furthermore, we establish the existence of suboptimal, distributed, and strictly stabilizing controllers for GSSs. Finally, we prove that both the optimal stability margin and the optimal cost in these systems vary in a Lipschitz continuous manner with respect to the system's parameters.

Image copy detection and retrieval from extensive databases is a prevalent challenge across numerous practical applications. To address this, we introduce a neural network designed to identify image copies by analyzing both pixel-level and high-level visual features. The network's efficacy is demonstrated through its performance on three significant copy detection benchmarks, where it surpasses current state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin. Furthermore, we present a specialized indexing strategy tailored for efficient copy retrieval, demonstrating that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and speed.

This study investigates information-theoretic authentication within a physical layer context where an adversary is present. The goal is to establish a rigorous definition of physical layer authentication and determine the necessary conditions for its successful implementation. Our analysis focuses on a model where the legitimate receiver and intruder experience distinct channel characteristics, specifically one where the signal-to-noise ratio at the adversary's end is lower than at the intended receiver's end. We derive the maximum achievable rate for unforgeable information transmission and demonstrate that when the adversary's channel capacity exceeds that of the legitimate receiver, a non-zero authenticable information rate can still be attained, provided the transmitter possesses side information. Furthermore, we examine a scenario where the adversary's channel is constrained by a finite state variable, showing that the maximum authenticable information rate can be derived using a single-letter optimization method.

We investigate the transition dynamics of Brownian particles initially at rest within a potential well when a constant driving force is applied. Our analysis focuses on the distribution of transition durations and the distribution of velocities immediately upon entering the "running" (escaped) state. We demonstrate that while velocity distributions are generally non-Gaussian, they approach a Gaussian profile only when the system is near the transition point. Furthermore, for both quasi-Gaussian and non-Gaussian scenarios, the distribution of velocities in the long-time limit aligns with the self-similar distribution derived by Lifshitz and Yakovenko. We also derive the cumulative distribution for transition durations, which exhibits a power-law tail at short times, transitioning to an exponential form at long times. Additionally, we examine the connection between the velocity distributions and the transition duration statistics.

This study examines the time-varying behavior of fiscal multipliers using a time-frequency Bayesian VAR model. The analysis reveals that contractionary fiscal shocks generate significantly larger responses to expansionary ones in normal economic conditions, whereas during recessions, both types of multipliers are generally insignificant. The observed variability in fiscal multiplier effects is primarily explained by shifts in the frequency of shocks rather than by a changing slope of the aggregate supply-demand curve. These empirical results are consistent with recent theoretical frameworks, including New Keynesian models featuring downward-sloping supply curves and imperfect competition, alongside theories based on imperfect information regarding fiscal policy.

We investigate the orbital angular momentum of a charge $e$ moving in a magnetic field $B$ within QED, specifically examining the contributions from radiative vacuum photons. These effects are analyzed using a non-covariant gauge-fixed QED framework in a two-dimensional spatial slice, where the photon propagator is chosen to be transverse to $B$ while other components are discarded. The calculation is performed via a semi-classical expansion of the QED action, treating the electron as a classical source. The resulting expressions for the orbital angular momentum components are derived as power series in $e^2$, with coefficients determined by Gaussian integrals over the free theory.

Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) involves classifying entity mentions into one of hundreds of distinct types based on their specific attributes. A primary challenge lies in the severe data sparsity affecting many type instances, alongside the difficulty of modeling complex word-type interactions. To address these issues, we propose a new framework embedding typology data into hyperbolic space, leveraging its capacity to represent hierarchical structures and variable-length paths. Our Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Network (HGConv) learns type-specific features by aggregating information from an entity's knowledge graph within the hyperbolic manifold. Furthermore, we developed a novel attention mechanism that dynamically adjusts feature importance based on learned typology embeddings. This approach surpasses state-of-the-art models on the CoNLL 2003 dataset, demonstrating significant performance gains.

This paper examines specific Hankel determinants associated with a new subclass of starlike functions, which are characterized by a condition involving the hypergeometric function $_2F_1$. Additionally, we derive additional results concerning the bounds of third-order coefficients ($|a_3|$ and $|a_4|$) and the third Hankel determinant ($|D_3(f)|$) for functions within this subclass.

Cloud data centers (CDCs) are increasingly vital for delivering services, yet their resource utilization remains suboptimal, causing significant financial losses for service providers. While traditional reactive load balancing relies on live migration to address overload, this approach incurs substantial costs due to the disruption of user applications. This paper introduces "Prepartition," an innovative strategy that proactively balances loads by isolating specific virtual machines (VMs) within overloaded hosts. These isolated VMs are then consolidated onto a single target host, freeing the source machine to accommodate new VMs. This process effectively increases the data center's capacity without interrupting active services. The paper details the prepartition algorithm, its implementation, and its evaluation through extensive simulations. Results indicate that compared to conventional load balancing methods, the prepartition approach can boost resource utilization by 10% to 15% while reducing user-perceived latency by 5% to 10%.

This paper investigates the computational difficulty of identifying correlated equilibria (CE) for a game defined by the intersection of several matroid structures. We establish that finding an $\alpha$-approximate Nash equilibrium ($\alpha$-NE) is NP-hard whenever $\alpha < O(\log^* n)$, where $n$ represents the number of agents. Furthermore, we demonstrate that determining an $\alpha$-correlated equilibrium ($\alpha$-CE) is NP-hard for any $\alpha < O(\sqrt{m}/\log m)$, with $m$ being the total count of constraints. In contrast, we present a polynomial-time algorithm capable of generating the intersection of two matroids that achieves a correlated equilibrium with an approximation factor of $\alpha$ = $O(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$. Additionally, we prove that an $\alpha$ = $O(\sqrt{m}/\log m)$-approximate CE can be computed in polynomial time for the scenario involving the intersection of an arbitrary matroid and a specific collection of range spaces derived from a set system.

This paper addresses the estimation of causal effects when covariates are partially observed through a mixture model, assuming data missing at random. We propose three methods: a standard maximum likelihood estimator, a multiple imputation estimator, and a novel class of covariate adjustment estimators. Although the first two methods are theoretically consistent, they are impractical for large-scale datasets due to the need to implete missing values. Our proposed estimator remains consistent and asymptotically normal while requiring no imputation, allowing it to handle large $n$ efficiently. It combines a doubly robust estimator for the conditional mean outcome with a nonparametric estimator for the propensity score, both of which utilize complete case data exclusively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach yields efficiency gains by leveraging partial observation data for either component. We also develop an algorithm for selecting optimal estimators within this class and conduct extensive simulations to evaluate finite-sample performance. Finally, we illustrate the method's application to estimating the causal effect of smoking on lung cancer incidence using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

Attacks targeting Industrial Control Systems (ICS) can result in severe consequences, including equipment damage, system malfunctions, and loss of life. While existing research predominantly examines threats to individual ICS components, this study investigates attacks leveraging compromised individual parts to jeopardize the entire process. To address this, we propose a new framework for risk assessment in interconnected ICS architectures. Our methodology employs a graph representation of these systems to model attack propagation, utilizing a specialized propagation matrix that accounts for both direct and indirect pathways. We validate this approach through an analysis of the North American electric power grid, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Document summarization is a well-established Natural Language Processing task that has seen significant research and commercial application, particularly in English. However, developing these models for Indian languages presents unique challenges due to their distinct linguistic structures, vocabularies, and cultural contexts. This paper introduces a comprehensive dataset for Marathi document summarization, featuring 1,000 articles paired with their respective high-quality human-generated summaries. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the inaugural dataset of its kind for Marathi summarization. We further evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art automatic summarization architectures on this new data.

This article introduces the concept of $S$-rings of Krull type and provides detailed characterizations along with properties and constructions for those of Krull type that are also of rank 3, 4, or 5. Additionally, it establishes necessary and sufficient conditions determining when such a Krull-type ring admits an automorphism of order 2.

This study reports the results of a high-precision astrometric campaign using the Gaia Data Release 2 (GDR2) catalog to investigate substellar companions around the nearby stars HIP 1481 and HIP 88399. For HIP 1481, a star with a mass of 0.84 $M_{\odot}$, we detected a significant residual in the proper motion parallax and astrometric likelihood maps, leading to a best-fitting solution that includes a companion with a mass of $10.5^{+1.5}_{-1.2} M_{Jup}$. This result is consistent with a previously identified candidate from the Gaia DR2 catalog, which suggested a potential companion of $11.5 \pm 1.5 M_{Jup}$. Similarly, for the nearby star HIP 88399 ($0.71 M_{\odot}$), our refined astrometric modeling reveals a pronounced residual in the posterior probability distribution, indicating a likely substellar companion of $11.5^{+2.0}_{-1.5} M_{Jup}$. These findings expand the inventory of known exoplanets and brown dwarfs within the Gaia DR2 catalog.

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for unsupervised learning, offering an unsupervised solution that complements traditional autoencoders by enhancing their reconstructive capabilities. This study introduces a supervised framework that leverages VAEs to facilitate zero-shot transfer learning. The proposed method trains a model to reconstruct inputs from their original distribution without utilizing any task-specific labels, thereby creating a robust, label-free foundation. Subsequently, a task-specific network is trained using this VAE-derived representation alongside the original input features. Empirical evaluations across various classification benchmarks demonstrate that this representation significantly improves generalization performance compared to standard baselines.

The rapid proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) has introduced novel security challenges, particularly within the domain of smart homes. While current research predominantly targets public blockchain integration for these networks, this study examines private blockchains instead. The authors argue that given the localized and controlled nature of residential environments, the superior customization, enhanced privacy, and heightened security offered by private blockchains make them a more suitable solution than public alternatives. Consequently, this paper presents a comprehensive security analysis of a private blockchain framework applied to a residential setting. The findings indicate that this approach effectively mitigates the primary security vulnerabilities inherent to IoT home networks.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning-based framework for optimizing the storage of Log-Likelihood Ratios (LLRs). Our proposed scheme involves training a neural network to reconstruct LLRs from their quantized versions, thereby generating an optimized mapping tailored to specific channel characteristics. This approach surpasses traditional uniform and Gaussian methods, delivering superior error-rate performance with a significantly reduced memory footprint. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this deep learning-driven strategy can be effectively applied to a wide range of channels, including those affected by Gaussian noise, additive discrete interference, and polarization-based architectures.

An upward planar drawing represents the vertices and edges of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) as pseudo-trees within the plane, maintaining the original graph's directionality. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for generating such drawings in linear time complexity, applicable to all upward planar drawings that do not include horizontal edges. The method's efficiency stems from a new structural characterization of these drawings, which also applies the approach to the problem of recognizing whether a given graph is upward planar.

Crowd-sourced image collections are frequently noisy, containing substantial amounts of irrelevant content that hinders the development of effective classifiers. This study introduces a two-stage pipeline designed to address two specific challenges: (1) the lack of a priori knowledge regarding the specific class labels within the dataset, and (2) the difficulty of handling massive volumes of crowd-sourced data. Our proposed method operates in two distinct phases. Initially, a two-step clustering algorithm groups the mixed images and their associated textual descriptions into coherent clusters. Subsequently, a one-hot encoding scheme converts these clusters into supervised labels, which are then utilized to train a classifier. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods on the MS COCO dataset.

This study examines a nonuniformly hyperbolic smooth semiflow defined on a compact manifold without applying Stefanov's framework. Instead, we establish that transfer operators acting on smooth observables exhibit non-uniform exponential decay in the Hölder norm, characterized specifically by the Hölder norm of these observables and the local stable expansion rates of the flow. This approach generalizes prior results by Barreira and Pesin, which addressed discrete time maps.

A covering array, denoted as [math]CA(N,t,k,lambda)[/math], is defined as an [math]Ntimes{math}k[/math] array with entries from a set of size [math]s[/math] that ensures every [math]ttimes{math}[/math] subarray contains each possible [math]t[/math]-tuple at least once. This study introduces the concept of [math]lambda[/math]-covering arrays, which require the [math]t[/math]-subarrays to contain each tuple at least once but not more than [math]lambda[/math] times. The primary objective is to determine the minimum [math]N[/math] for given parameters [math]s,t,k[/math] and [math]lambda[/math] and to explore the application of these arrays in the design of experiments.

We introduce a novel class of nonlocal games where the winning probability for the optimal strategy is bounded from below by the squared state fidelity. Applied to the study of the best attainable winning probabilities for the CHSH game under noise, our approach offers a fresh perspective on the derivation of Bell inequalities involving the squared state fidelity. Additionally, our method yields a fresh proof for the well-established result that the optimal winning probability for the CHSH game decreases linearly with the state's noise level.

Although the JCHARMING paper introduced EvoCRASH, a state-of-the-art evolutionary crash reproduction technique for Java applications, fully replicating its results remains challenging due to the complexity of the original experiments. This study evaluates EvoCRASH's performance against a new dataset of 1,000 crashes from 20 Java programs, comparing it to the original study's 200 crashes from 10 programs. We conducted a direct replication of JCHARMING experiments using identical configurations and a newly developed crash reproduction tool, CRAMER, which simplifies the process by automatically generating mutation operators. Results indicate that both EvoCRASH and JCHARMING could reproduce 17% of all crashes in the new dataset. However, CRAMER achieved this with a significantly lower computational cost, requiring only 1.5% of the time and 1.1% of the memory that EvoCRASH consumed.

We investigate the impact of viscous corrections on the yield and anisotropic flow of thermal photons produced during heavy-ion collisions. Although viscosity dampens the hydrodynamic flow anisotropies responsible for these yields and flow coefficients, the thermal nature of the photons allows the impact of these corrections to outweigh the viscous suppression effects. Consequently, the yield of thermal photons is expected to rise rather than decrease.

This study examines regular magnetic orders (RMO) in spin models featuring O(3) spin rotation symmetry, specifically focusing on the RMO's stability against general symmetry-breaking perturbations. We demonstrate that RMOs are robust, a property that supports the classification of magnetic structures in the "magnetic atom" framework. Additionally, we highlight the RMOs' utility in facilitating the analysis of spin-wave spectra.

The primary goal of A/B testing is to determine if an average treatment effect (ATE) exists. Although many firms rely on a standard approach, this method often necessitates extensive sample sizes to identify meaningful ATEs. To overcome this limitation, some organizations are exploring adaptive designs that enhance ATE detection. However, a significant hurdle for these adaptive designs is the potential compromise of statistical validity due to the multiplicity of design decisions made during the study. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework for adaptive A/B tests that ensures rigorous validity. The proposed method models the impact of design modifications on the noncentrality parameter of the test statistic and incorporates this into an informative prior for the ATE. The demonstration utilizes data from a real-world scenario, showing that this approach can boost the power of detection by up to 20% while maintaining valid inference.

The foundational equations governing cosmological inflation are the Friedmann and Klein-Gordon equations. The slow-roll parameters serve as a method to quantify the degree of the slow-roll approximation. By examining the variations among different definitions of these parameters, we analyze their impact on parameter estimation within slow-roll models. Additionally, we compare parameter estimation outcomes derived from numerical solutions of the equations against those obtained using the slow-roll approximation.

The CDF II collaboration recently announced a precise $W$ boson mass measurement of $206,569 \pm 6.3$ MeV, which represents a $5.3\sigma$ deviation from the Standard Model prediction. Given that this measurement relies heavily on jet energy reconstruction, our analysis investigates the role of jet substructure in enhancing $W$ boson mass measurements through both simulation and real $pp$ collision data from $2011$ to $2018$. We observe that utilizing the energy distribution of jet substructure observables can significantly lower systematic uncertainties. Furthermore, we present a novel method for determining the $W$ boson mass using the transverse momentum distribution of the jet resulting from a leptonically decaying $W$ boson.

Software developers frequently struggle to identify suitable search terms when addressing specific issues via change request (CR) searches. To overcome this, we introduce a novel approach that automatically generates a list of search term candidates from the titles and descriptions of similar past CRs. Our system employs a two-stage framework: first, a two-pass term extraction method identifies candidate keywords, and second, a two-class classification model determines the final set of relevant search terms. We conducted an empirical study evaluating this approach with 162 software engineers across 1,024 distinct CRs. Results indicate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing baseline methods, achieving an F1-score of 0.70.

This study investigates the link between speaker entrainment and the acoustic features of their communication. We propose that entrainment manifests in acoustic characteristics as a form of dynamic alignment, proposing a novel Dynamic Alignment Index (DAI) to quantify it. By applying this metric to the ACI Dialogue Intelligence Challenge 2021 dataset, we demonstrate that the proposed DAI effectively captures both proposed and unlabeled behaviors of the speakers. Additionally, we evaluate the index's reliability through a validation process involving lab-based recordings of six participants, confirming its robustness.

Spectral energy distributions (SEDs) are essential for analyzing galaxies, yet the sheer volume of available data makes it difficult to derive physical properties from them. This study introduces a novel method for modeling SEDs that utilizes a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach to solve the inverse problem. By employing a flexible polynomial basis to represent the spectral energy distribution, we aim to improve the accuracy of galaxy property estimation. We test this methodology using synthetic data and the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) Main Galaxy Sample, comparing our results against established models. This work demonstrates that the proposed technique is both accurate and reliable, and we provide the associated software as an open-source tool for the research community.

Temporal action localization involves identifying specific actions within video frames, a challenge for which deep learning-based supervised methods currently achieve state-of-the-art results. However, these approaches demand extensive manual annotation, rendering them impractical for numerous real-world scenarios. This paper introduces SSCAP, an unsupervised method designed to automatically identify actions by analyzing representative features extracted from video segments. The core of SSCAP lies in a novel cross-modal attention mechanism that dynamically integrates information from both spatial and temporal domains. This mechanism dynamically adjusts the significance of individual frames and video segments based on their relevance to one another, thereby enhancing the model's ability to recognize actions effectively. Experimental evaluations across three prominent datasets demonstrate that SSCAP surpasses other leading unsupervised methods, improving performance by 10.5%, 11.3%, and 12.3% on ActivityNet, Kinetics-400, and Charades respectively. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzhengzheng

This study investigates the low-lying hadronic states composed of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, specifically searching for hadronic molecular configurations. Our analysis reveals that the $D^* \Sigma_c$ system hosts two molecular states, identified as $Z_{c0}^+(2900)^{+}$ and $Z_{c1}^+(2900)^{+}$, with the latter being a $D^* \Sigma_c$ molecule. Additionally, the $D \Sigma_c$ system contains two molecular states, $Z_{c0}(2000)^{0}$ and $Z_{c0}^{\prime}(2000)^{0}$, where the former is a $D \Sigma_c$ molecule and the other is a $D^* \Sigma_c$ molecule. We have calculated the masses, decay constants, and decay widths for these states, with decay widths determined by evaluating the relevant decay channels. Our findings indicate that the $D \Sigma_c$ molecule $Z_{c0}(2000)^{0}$ is highly sensitive to the $D \Sigma_c$ binding energy, which is heavily influenced by the quark mass of the charm quark. Furthermore, the $D \Sigma_c$ system may support a $D \Sigma_c$ molecular state with a $J^P = 3/2^+$ quantum number.

In recent years, the integration of testing into the computer science curriculum has gained significant attention. However, current educational practices often rely on the "waterfall" approach, where testing is introduced only after students master the concept of bugs. This study instead proposes an alternative strategy that incorporates testing from the outset, utilizing inquiry-based learning (IBL) methods. Through a pilot experiment, the authors evaluated the efficacy of these IBL approaches in fostering the development of testing concepts among students. The results indicate that both the pedagogical design and execution of IBL activities can be refined to further enhance student learning outcomes.

Domain Adaptation (DA) addresses the challenge of adapting to an unlabeled target domain when source domain data is available. This work introduces Semi-Supervised Mutual Enhancement (MUSE), a novel framework that leverages the underutilized potential of extensive unlabeled target data through two primary mechanisms. First, it employs semi-supervised learning to acquire target samples and generate pseudo-labels, which are then used to train a model capable of transferring robust representations from the source domain. Second, to further strengthen this cross-domain alignment, the method incorporates an enhanced mutual enhancement technique that encourages consistent feature representations across domains. The framework's efficacy is validated through extensive experiments on three standard benchmarks, where it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The code implementation can be accessed at: https://github.com/zhengzhu1/MUSE.

A Gas Core Reactor (GCR) is a proposed nuclear system designed to produce electricity through the rotation of a massive, non-spontaneous spinning rotor driven by the resulting thermal expansion gases. This research investigates the structural integrity of the GCR's gas component using a 3D finite element model, analyzing how varying operational parameters influence rotor spin. The analysis examines the impact of different rotational speeds, fuel density, and fuel composition on the structural stability of the spinning rotor. Furthermore, a power generation formula is derived to calculate the electrical output of the system.

We introduce a novel approach for localizing particle interactions within a gas-phase time projection chamber (TPC) using a Domain-informed Neural Network (DiNN). This method incorporates the problem's geometric constraints directly into the neural network architecture, enabling the DiNN to model the physical topology of drift electrons. We evaluate the DiNN against a traditional multilayer perceptron (MLP) across simulated events from the LHC, Belle II, and future hadron collider (FHC) environments. Results demonstrate that the MLP achieves comparable performance in LHC and Belle II scenarios. However, under the high-density electron conditions typical of the FHC, the MLP fails to converge, whereas the DiNN remains effective. Consequently, the proposed Domain-informed framework offers a robust, generalizable solution for future TPC designs.

We introduce a new substellar atmosphere model that accounts for the temperature dependence of molecular absorption cross-sections. This approach yields substantial shifts in predicted atmospheric spectra, including altered absorption band depths, modified atmospheric depths, and the emergence of new features. We demonstrate that these adjustments are essential for accurately interpreting both current and upcoming observational data.

This paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of the standard grounding procedure in Answer Set Programming, specifically focusing on the well-foundedness of the underlying well-founded operator. We demonstrate that this operator can be formulated as a monotonic operator defined on a specific lattice. Establishing its existence and defining its behavior yields a framework that subsumes the semantics of the least fixed point, the fixed point, and the least Herbrand model. Furthermore, the discussion extends to the semantics of the stable model and the stable Herbrand model. Ultimately, the proposed approach provides a unified perspective on the semantics of the stable model and the least Herbrand model within the context of the abstract grounding process.

We establish a comprehensive framework for handling multiple resources, demonstrating that the distances based on relative entropy to invariant sets serve as robust metrics for resource quantification. Our analysis further clarifies the trade-offs inherent in converting resources from one type to another and establishes conditions for the existence of canonical quantum ground states. Additionally, we explore the connection between these multi-parameter schemes and resource theories characterized by single operator relative entropy, providing a detailed examination of how symmetries and their respective generators are linked.

This study examines the noncoherent minimum mean-square error estimation (PMMSE) of Gaussian signals, focusing on its relationship with power control and its potential to exceed standard MMSE in certain setups. It is demonstrated that P and control can align when the channel's magnitude follows a Rayleigh distribution, yet they diverge in cases involving deterministic fading. Furthermore, the paper establishes that the gradient of P and control with respect to P and control power can be expressed as a weighted average of squared fading magnitudes, where the weights are determined by the MMSE itself. These findings are subsequently leveraged to develop an iterative algorithm for computing P and control power, with performance validated through numerical simulations.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for identifying the number of common stochastic trends within cointegrated systems. Our approach relies on establishing a theoretical limit regarding the proportion of eigenvalues smaller than a specific threshold of the estimated first-m transition matrix of differences, where this threshold is determined using a bootstrap technique. Our findings demonstrate that this method attains asymptotic statistical consistency. Furthermore, our empirical evaluation shows that the technique performs comparably to existing methods under both null and alternative hypotheses.

Low-density parity-check codes are favored for quantum error correction due to their efficient decoding algorithms and compatibility with scalable hardware. This study introduces a class of quasi-cyclic low-rate LDPC codes, demonstrating that they achieve the same distance scaling as other LDPC codes when the block length increases. We further show that these codes possess a constant weight as the block length approaches infinity.

A subset $D$ of vertices in a graph $G$ constitutes a distance-$r$ dominating set if the $r$-neighborhood of $D$ encompasses all vertices in $G$. The minimum size of such a set is denoted by $\gamma_r(G)$. This study establishes that determining $\gamma_r(G)$ is NP-hard for every fixed $r \ge 1$ within the class of interval graphs. Additionally, we demonstrate that the problem remains hard even when $r=1$ and $G$ is restricted to the class of chordal bipartite graphs.

Topological states in two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators (HOTTIs) are typically understood as being protected by a bulk gap, yet this protection fails in the presence of disorder, leading to the decay of corner states. We demonstrate that, in chiral systems, this protection is actually derived from anti-bonding gaps rather than bulk insulation, and these anti-bonding gaps remain intact under disorder. We validate this concept using the 2D Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, where we show that transport through the decayed corner states is dominated by hopping between the neighboring bulk and the states themselves. We further show that this mechanism extends to non-chiral systems, with the decay occurring between the bulk and the corner states mediated by a finite hopping amplitude.

This work outlines the results of ATLAS's ATLAS collaboration's search for heavy gluinos within two specific regions of the supersymmetry parameter space, utilizing proton-proton collisions recorded by the ATLAS detector at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The first analysis targets gluino pair production decaying into bottom quarks and neutralinos, which subsequently decay into leptons and missing energy; this region is optimized for scenarios where the mass difference between the gluino and the lighter neutralino exceeds 100 GeV. The second region addresses the case of a smaller mass difference, specifically below 100 GeV, by focusing on final states containing bottom quarks, b-tagged jets, and significant amounts of missing transverse momentum. No significant excess over Standard Model predictions was observed, leading to the exclusion of gluino masses up to 2.2 TeV in the high-mass difference scenario and up to 1.8 TeV in the low-magnitude difference scenario, assuming the simplified model benchmark points used.

We introduce a four-dimensional light field model trained on a four-dimensional light field representation, which encodes both per-pixel color and the associated spatial and temporal viewing directions. This directionally embedded appearance data is synthesized through a convolutional neural network that integrates features from pre-computed light field representations. Our approach offers two primary benefits: (1) the ability to synthesize new views without relying on any specific parametric model for motion, and (2) the capacity to generate high-resolution, temporally smooth views even when the input data consists of sparse viewpoints. We validate this method on real-world datasets featuring sparse views, demonstrating that it produces convincing results for scenes with limited angular coverage.

We introduce a new method for observing and tracking orbital dynamics in close binary systems, leveraging the fact that their light curves exhibit periodic modulations. By applying Fourier analysis to these patterns, we can derive orbital periods even when the orbits are highly eccentric. This approach was tested on the system V1298 Cgn using the Gaia EDR3 dataset; the results confirm the system's 1.6-year orbital period and align with findings from previous studies. Furthermore, this technique offers a means to identify potential exoplanets orbiting single stars, as well as to refine the parameters of known exoplanetary systems.

We demonstrate that the gravitational sector of the color-kinematics duality is governed by the algebra of area-preserving diffeomorphisms, a result that emerges from the self-dul formulation of gravity. This insight provides a fresh perspective on the gravitational κ-algebra and its connection to the Wess-Zumino consistency equation.

Solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) generate type II radio bursts, which serve as a reliable indicator of shock waves propagating through the solar corona. Although these events are frequent, pinpointing their exact locations remains difficult. This study introduces a novel method to locate type II burst sources by analyzing the timing of substructures within the bursts alongside radio images of the CME. The method relies on a model that simulates type II bursts using a two-component mechanism: a forward shock driving type III bursts and an associated type II emission component from the shock front itself. By comparing the simulated time profiles with actual radio data, we identify the optimal source position that best matches the observations. The method's accuracy was validated using synthetic data generated from a 3D MHD model of a flaring CME event. When applied to real observational data from the 2017 December 13 CME event captured by the Dynamic Spectrograph on the STEREO/WAVES instrument, the technique successfully located the type II burst sources within the CME's wake.
